title: Texas Republicans spent billions lowering property taxes. What can Democrats do differently? (page title/URL slug: 'Texas Democrats consider tax relief for homeowners and renters')

verdict_reason: The only LVT content is one 4-paragraph passage in an 'Other ideas to lower taxes' section: Lars Doucet (Center for Land Economics cofounder, Tier 2 advocate) suggests the state could let localities experiment with an LVT. No Democrat, caucus, bill, hearing or platform plank proposes or endorses an LVT; the article presents it as an expert idea, not a Democratic proposal. The CLE 'estimates' are paraphrased, unquantified and drawn from 'other parts of the country', not Texas. The Houston/Pennsylvania sentence adds no fact beyond what places/texas.md and events/houston-plan-of-taxation.md already carry. Under EDITORIAL 4c a news article earns a place only for a new verifiable fact or event on LVT; the Democratic items it does report (Hinojosa, Bernal, Bhojani, Goodwin proposals) are real named-legislator facts but are general property-tax relief, outside the wiki's LVT scope and not tied to land taxation. Optional low-value alternative: a single clause on texas.md noting that the Tribune reported the LVT idea was raised only by an advocate and no Democratic official has proposed it; not recommended.
claim_grade: B-claim for the reported facts (named officials' statements and proposals, via a major nonprofit newsroom); the LVT passage is D/Tier 2 (Doucet, Center for Land Economics, origin/proponent only); Houston sentence is B-claim secondary and consistent with existing A/B sources.
content_summary: Frame: after the Nov 2026 election, Democrats 'haven't completely fleshed out their property tax agenda'; they have 'gestured broadly' at extending homeowner tax breaks and direct relief for the state's 4.1 million renters. Mostly interviews and individual member proposals; no caucus document, hearing or interim charge is cited.

Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned on ending state corporate subsidies to fund cuts; said in an August interview she would bring residential property taxes 'as low as possible, and if we can eliminate them, I would be for that.' Has not specified which breaks or whether school taxes only.

Rep. Diego Bernal (D-San Antonio, vice chair House Public Education): proposal to cap homeowners' school property taxes after 15 years in the same house if the bill rose 120%. Lt. Gov.-elect Vikki Goodwin floated limiting how fast rental properties' values can rise in exchange for lower rents. Rep. Salman Bhojani (D-Euless): renter payment up to 10% of prior-year rent for 12+ months at the address. Rep. Trey Martinez Fischer (D-San Antonio, vice chair House Ways and Means): 'Texas doesn't have a revenue problem.' Republican side: Rep. Brent Money (R-Greenville) on corporate welfare; Rep. Matt Shaheen (R-Plano) sales-tax-for-property-tax swap; Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick balks at abolition.

Figures: state committed to $51 billion of property tax cuts per biennium; school districts collected $29.7 billion M&O taxes last year; homeowners' share of school M&O about $8.6 billion (Comptroller revenue estimator Tetyana Melnyk), rising to $12 billion by 2032; $52 billion a year in sales tax breaks (John Diamond, Baker Institute); voters rejected about 80% of 3 Nov local rate-raising measures; about 60% of homeowners 65+ pay no school property tax; roughly $1 billion forgone to data-center abatements vs $1.4 billion paid in 2024.
Other ideas section: circuit breaker (Shannon Halbrook, Every Texan); LVT (Doucet); more housing; data centers (Jennifer Rabb, TTARA).

LVT passage verbatim essentials: 'The state could consider allowing localities to experiment with enacting what's called a "land value" tax, which taxes land but not buildings, said Lars Doucet, who cofounded the Center for Land Economics, a nonprofit think tank that advocates for the tax.' Doucet says it could 'potentially lower taxes for the typical homeowner as well as for renters,' 'citing estimates the center has conducted in other parts of the country,' but homes on large lots 'may wind up paying more.' It could push owners of vacant land and parking lots to sell or build. Quote: 'You really do push the tax burden onto vacant, undeveloped lots, particularly in these city centers' (Doucet).

Constitutional/Houston passage: 'Few places in the country have enacted a pure land value tax. But some places in Pennsylvania allow land to be taxed at a different rate than buildings — what's known as a "split roll." Houston enacted a split assessment in the 1910s, but an appeals court overturned it, citing the state's requirement that property taxation be "equal and uniform."' No Article VIII citation, no case name, no indication any Democrat has considered the barrier; the article does not say Democrats are considering an LVT.
